mappings.note: The shloka invoking Ganga, Yamuna and the other rivers into ritual water. A religious invocation, so LO-150; not LO-146, because no conservation is at issue.
'Amrita manthana' as the churning of the cosmic ocean, the legend behind the Kumbh sites. Religious mythology under LO-150.
Ficus religiosa identified as the Peepul, held sacred across faiths. Grouped with the sacred-tree and grove items under conservation of flora, since a protected species is the subject.
Sacred groves conserving local biodiversity and ecosystems. The conservation outcome in its plainest form.
Sacred geography treating the land as inherently divine. A religious idea; LO-146 would fit an item about acting to protect that land.
Matches Sabarimala, Girnar, Rameswaram and the Golden Temple to their traditions. Religious traditions and their sacred sites.
Pilgrimage routes serving as trade conduits, with merchants and pilgrims exchanging goods and ideas. Economic and cultural history, so the history goal.

A matching set spanning the Kumbh and Pandharpur wari as pilgrimages (LO-150), sacred ecology as conservation through reverence (LO-146) and the Uttarapatha as a trade route (CG-SST2). All three lanes are needed because the item deliberately mixes them.
Names pilgrimage or tirthayatra. Religious practice under LO-150.
Names 'shrine' for a place holy by association with the divine. Religious vocabulary; not LO-149, since no building style is described.
Names a Buddhist sacred site. A sacred-site recall of one tradition.
Names takhts as the Sikh seats of spiritual authority. Religious institution, so LO-150 rather than the administration outcome, which concerns kingdoms.
Names one of the Sikh takhts. Same religious-tradition lane as its companion item.
The literal sense of 'tirtha' as a crossing place, which the chapter uses to explain the religious idea. Kept with the other tirtha items under LO-150.
Tirthankaras as the preachers of dharma linked to Jain tirthas. Doctrine of a tradition.
Names a Jain sacred site. A sacred-site recall, so LO-150.
Ayyappa as the deity of Sabarimala. Religious tradition; the item does not touch the temple's construction, so not LO-149.
Names the Pandharpur wari. A pilgrimage tradition, not a poetry item, so LO-151 does not apply.
Bhudevi as Mother Earth in Hinduism. A religious personification, as with the other Bhudevi items.
The Dongria Khond as the community that holds Niyam Dongar sacred. A tradition-and-site recall, so LO-150; the grove items about protection carry LO-146.
Studying trade routes and the goods and encounters along them to show socio-economic and cultural connection. Historical method and economic history, so the goal.
Matches sites to their religious significance and rejects Bodh Gaya as the place of the first sermon. Religious traditions throughout.
Rejects the claim that sacred geography is uniquely Indian, citing Greek, Native American and Maori parallels. A comparative point about religious ideas, so LO-150.
Statements on the Nadistuti hymn, the Pandharpur wari's deity and Toda reverence for Nilgiri peaks. Religious traditions across three examples.
The hard trek to a hill shrine read as a figure for the inner path. Religious meaning, so LO-150.
A Tirthankara as a liberated soul and 'ford-maker' who shows the path. Jain doctrine under LO-150.
Pilgrimage bringing people of different regions and languages together into a shared heritage. A consequence of religious practice, so LO-150; CG-SST2 was used for the trade-route items instead.
Jyotirlingas of Shiva against Shakti Pithas of the goddess. A distinction within religious tradition.
Matching keyed on tirtha as a symbolic crossing to a higher state. Religious concept under LO-150.
A forest protected for ancestral spirits, preserving unique plants and animals, has to be named a sacred grove. Conservation of flora and fauna carries the answer.
Sorts the real purposes of a tirthayatra from purely commercial travel. Religious practice, so LO-150 even though trade is the distractor.
Ayyappa as the deity of the Sabarimala pilgrimage. Religious tradition, the twin of the earlier Sabarimala item.
The Peepul called Bodhi because the Buddha was enlightened beneath it. The religious meaning of the tree, so LO-150 rather than the flora-conservation reading given to the botanical item.
A takht as a seat of authority against a gurdwara as a place of worship. A distinction inside a religious tradition.
Completes the name of the Pandharpur wari. Pilgrimage-tradition recall under LO-150.
Toda protection of Shola forests read as traditional ecological wisdom conserving a rare ecosystem. Conservation sensitivity, so LO-146.
A three-month journey from the north to Rameswaram and back identified as tirthayatra. Pilgrimage practice under LO-150.
Judges which natural features are usually treated as tirthas and which are not. A question about how sacredness is assigned, so LO-150.
The Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya as a descendant of the original. A sacred-site and tradition recall, so LO-150.
Defines UNESCO's 'intangible heritage' as living traditions and practices. A heritage-and-sources concept, so the history goal rather than a religious idea.
